notes.headline: TJX: comparable sales up 4% and above plan, with the stock up 8% on a stronger holiday outlook
notes.takeaway: Sales rose 6% to $16.0 billion and comparable sales grew 4%. Adjusted EPS of $1.34 matched the consensus exactly, so the 8% jump in the shares was about the tone: every division grew, the international business accelerated to 8%, and management expects the core US chain to improve further in the holiday quarter.
results: TJX reported net sales of $16.0 billion for the quarter ended October 31, up 6%, with consolidated comparable sales up 4%, above the company’s plan. Reported earnings per share were $1.39, up 9%; excluding a five-cent net benefit from tariff refunds, adjusted EPS was $1.34, up 5% and in line with the consensus of $1.34.

By division, comparable sales rose 2% at Marmaxx — TJ Maxx and Marshalls in the US — against a 6% increase a year ago, 5% at HomeGoods, 6% at TJX Canada and 8% at TJX International, up from 3% a year earlier. Adjusted pretax margin was 12.5%, down 0.2 points on last year but above plan.

Inventory was $9.8 billion against $9.4 billion, flat on a per-store basis. The company added 64 stores in the quarter to reach 5,349 and returned $1.5 billion to shareholders through buybacks and dividends.
mgmt: Chief executive Ernie Herrman said sales, profitability and earnings per share all exceeded expectations, and that the results show the benefit of a global, diversified business. He said unseasonably warm weather in the US and Canada had been holding back demand in some categories, but that the company expects sales momentum to accelerate through the holiday season and further improvement at Marmaxx in the fourth quarter.

For the fourth quarter TJX plans comparable sales up 2% to 3%, an adjusted pretax margin of 11.8% to 11.9% and adjusted EPS of $1.42 to $1.45. For the full year it now expects comparable sales up 4% and adjusted EPS of $5.17 to $5.20, with adjusted pretax margin still at 12.0% to 12.1%.

Two accounting points were flagged. The company received refunds of tariffs paid under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, which lift reported profit, and it is accruing extra incentive compensation related to those refunds, which will weigh on the fourth quarter. The outlook also now assumes higher fuel costs than before.
view: The first thing to understand about this report is that the earnings number was not the story. Adjusted EPS matched the consensus to the cent, which normally produces a shrug. The shares rose 8% because investors had been worried about Marmaxx — the US core, about 60% of sales — where comparable growth had slowed to 2%. Management saying that improvement is coming in the quarter that matters most, and that warm weather rather than a weaker shopper explains the softness, removed the worry that the engine was stalling.

The quality of the quarter is in how broad it was. HomeGoods at 5%, Canada at 6% and the international business at 8% are all stronger than the US apparel chain, and the international acceleration from 3% to 8% is the most interesting figure in the release. TK Maxx in Europe has long been the less profitable sibling; if it is now growing fastest, the argument that TJX has a long runway outside the United States gets stronger. A retailer with 5,349 stores still opening 64 in a quarter is not a mature one.

Off-price retail has a peculiar advantage that this environment suits. TJX buys what other retailers and brands cannot sell, so disruption elsewhere — tariffs, cancelled orders, department stores closing — improves its supply. Management’s phrase about ‘outstanding availability’ of merchandise is that advantage stated plainly. Inventory flat per store, while sales rise, says the buyers are being selective rather than loading up, which protects the margin.

The reason for some restraint is the margin itself. Adjusted pretax margin fell 0.2 points and the fourth-quarter guide of 11.8% to 11.9% includes higher fuel costs and extra incentive pay. The tariff refunds are a one-off that should be ignored, as the company itself does. At a valuation in the high twenties to low thirties of earnings for mid-single-digit comparable growth and about 9% adjusted EPS growth, TJX is priced as the dependable compounder it has been for decades — fairly, not cheaply, and the premium rests on that dependability continuing.
notes.watch: Marmaxx comparable sales in the holiday quarter. Management has committed to an improvement from 2%; if it arrives, the weather explanation holds, and if it does not, the question about the US shopper comes straight back.
